No, not by itself, according to the project's Ludion lessons (`.ludion/lessons.md`). With wrangler 4.122.0 or later, which is what's installed here (4.148.0), `nodejs_compat` is on by default if your `compatibility_date` is 2026-08-04 or later. To turn it off you need two steps:

1. Remove any positive flags (`nodejs_compat`, `nodejs_compat_v2`) from `compatibility_flags`.
2. Add **both** `no_nodejs_compat` and `no_nodejs_compat_v2`.

The change is silent. If you only add `no_nodejs_compat`, you get no error, so the Worker can still have Node.js APIs without you noticing. I haven't tested this myself; it comes from that lesson. To confirm it, run `wrangler dev` and check whether something like `node:buffer` still imports.

Pass `--latest`: `npx wrangler versions upload --latest`. In wrangler 4.124.0 and later (you have 4.148.0), `--latest` uses the newest compatibility date your installed Wrangler supports, so it doesn't reach for a runtime date newer than your CLI. Don't also set `--compatibility-date` on the command line, because that pins a specific date.

This project's `.ludion/lessons.md` notes that a compatibility date of 2026-08-04 or later turns `nodejs_compat` on by default. If you don't want that, remove the `nodejs_compat` flags and add both `no_nodejs_compat` and `no_nodejs_compat_v2` to `compatibility_flags`.

You set the jurisdiction with the `--jurisdiction` flag on `wrangler d1 create`, for example `wrangler d1 create my-db --jurisdiction eu`. The values are `eu` (European Union), `fedramp` (FedRAMP-compliant data centers), and `us` (United States). `us` was added in wrangler 4.121.0, so it works with the 4.148.0 installed here.

Setting `X_LOCAL_OBSERVABILITY=false` turns off local observability capture in `wrangler dev`. Since wrangler 4.118.0, `wrangler dev` records request traces and console logs by default and shows them in the Observability tab of the Local Explorer. With this variable set to `false`, nothing is captured and that tab stays empty. Your Worker runs exactly the same either way. Only the local tracing and log collection is skipped.

The limit applies to the **compressed (gzip) size** of your Worker, not the raw size. Wrangler prints both after a build or `--dry-run` (`Total Upload: … KiB / gzip: … KiB`), and the gzip number is the one checked against the limit. That limit is **3 MB on the Workers Free plan and 10 MB on the Paid plan**. Separately, the uncompressed bundle can't be larger than 64 MB.

This comes from what I know about Cloudflare's published limits, not from a docs check today, and the project's Ludion lessons don't mention it. If you're close to the line, confirm the current numbers on the Workers "Limits" page. To see where the size comes from, `wrangler deploy --dry-run --outdir dist --metafile` shows which dependencies take up the most space.

Your installed wrangler (4.148.0) no longer accepts the `legacy_env` field. Its config validation now treats any `legacy_env` key as an error, which is why deploys fail (`node_modules/wrangler/wrangler-dist/cli.js:20314`). Service environments have been removed. Each environment now deploys as its own Worker named `<name>-<environment>`, which is what `legacy_env = true` already did, and that was the default. So the fix is to delete the line. Nothing else changes, and your Worker deploys the same way as before.

The config should look like this, with any `env` blocks kept as they are:

```jsonc
{
  "name": "bench-worker",
  "main": "src/index.js",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-10-01"
}
```

The `wrangler.jsonc` in this directory already looks like that and has no `legacy_env`. If deploys still fail, check whether a different config file or an environment-specific one still sets it.

According to that file, wrangler 4.141.0 added `--durable-objects-code-update-mode` to `wrangler deploy`. It sets how new code reaches Durable Object instances that are already running. If you don't pass it, wrangler uses the **deferred** strategy: running instances switch to the new code within at most 5 minutes rather than immediately. To set the behaviour permanently instead of per deploy, use `durable_objects.code_update_strategy` in your wrangler config.

The file doesn't list the other values the flag accepts, so `npx wrangler deploy --help` is the way to confirm them on your version (4.148.0).

Use two wrangler commands:

- **Bundle size:** `npx wrangler deploy --dry-run --outdir dist` builds the Worker without deploying it. It prints the total and gzipped upload size, and writes the bundled output to `dist/` so you can check what's taking up space. Add `--metafile` to get an esbuild metafile, which you can load into a bundle analyzer.
- **Startup time:** `npx wrangler check startup` builds your Worker and profiles its startup locally. It writes a `worker-startup.cpuprofile` file, which you can open in Chrome DevTools (Performance tab) or VS Code to see where time goes during global-scope initialization. Pass `--args` to profile with your usual build flags, or `--worker-bundle` to profile a bundle you've already built.

When you actually deploy, wrangler also prints the measured "Worker Startup Time" next to the upload size. Comparing that number against the local profile is a good sanity check.

Yes. Each workflow entry has a `concurrency.limit` setting, which is the most Workflow instances that can run at the same time. It was added in wrangler 4.127.0. The config schema of your installed wrangler 4.148.0 includes it (`node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json`, around line 4025):

```toml
[[workflows]]
name = "my-workflow"
binding = "MY_WORKFLOW"
class_name = "MyWorkflow"

[workflows.concurrency]
limit = 10
```

In `wrangler.jsonc` it's `"concurrency": { "limit": 10 }` inside the workflow object. Don't confuse it with the separate `limits` block, which holds other per-workflow limits, or with `max_concurrency` on Queue consumers.

A `connect` handler is a Worker entry point, next to `fetch` and `scheduled`, that receives raw TCP socket connections instead of HTTP requests. You export it as `connect(socket, env, ctx)` on your default export, then read from and write to the socket directly. In wrangler (4.125.0 or later; you have 4.148.0 installed), you add a `connect` entry to your config with `protocol` set to `tcp` and a `port`. `wrangler dev` then listens on that port and sends incoming connections to your handler.

In `wrangler versions secret bulk`, setting a secret's value to `null` in the JSON input removes that secret from the new Worker version that the command creates. Secrets with string values are added or updated as usual, so one bulk call can both set and delete secrets.

This behavior was added in wrangler 4.148.0, which is the version this project has installed. Older versions don't support deleting secrets with `null`.

Yes, that's expected. `this.queue()` doesn't run your callback inside the request that queued it. It saves the callback's method name and a JSON-serializable payload to the Agent's SQLite storage, then runs it later from the queue loop. That can happen after the original request has finished, or even after the Durable Object has hibernated and woken up again. So inside the callback, `getCurrentAgent()` gives you the agent, but `request` (and usually `connection`) is `undefined`. A live `Request` object can't be saved to storage anyway.

The fix is to copy what you need from the request into the payload when you queue it, for example `this.queue("process", { userId, url: request.url, authHeader })`, and read it from the payload in the callback. Don't store secrets in the payload unless you're comfortable having them saved in the Agent's storage.

I answered from how the Agents SDK works, not from your code or the installed `agents` 0.27.0 source. If the callback can't see the agent itself either, that's a different problem and worth looking into.

An Agent works out its own name from the Durable Object ID (`ctx.id.name`), and only IDs made with `idFromName()` or `getByName()` carry a name. If you address it with `idFromString()`, `newUniqueId()`, or a name longer than 1,024 bytes, the ID has no name. So when your RPC method touches anything that needs `this.name`, the Agent throws: "could not determine its Durable Object name. Address it with idFromName() or getByName()…" (`node_modules/agents/dist/lifecycle-CFu6OV03.js:1097`). To fix it, get the stub by name with `env.MyAgent.getByName(name)`, `getAgentByName(env.MyAgent, name)`, or `idFromName(name)`. If this happens under `wrangler dev`, also update Wrangler/workerd and use a current `compatibility_date`, since older runtimes don't expose `ctx.id.name` at all.

To use Cap'n Web, pass `transport: "capnweb"` when you create the client, e.g. `new AgentClient({ agent: "MyAgent", name: "room-1", transport: "capnweb" })`. The same option works on `useAgent`. If you leave it out, the client uses `"cf-websocket"`, a hibernating WebSocket where `call()` sends JSON `rpc` frames.

With `"capnweb"`, protocol frames travel over a Cap'n Web session. The host's `callables` (an `RpcTarget` set in the WebSockets capability options) are served as native Cap'n Web methods on the session root. That means `client.call()` and `client.stub.method()` invoke them directly, calls can pipeline, a returned `ReadableStream` streams, and a returned `RpcTarget` comes back as a live stub.

There are three caveats, all from the type definitions in your installed `agents` 0.27.0 (`node_modules/agents/dist/client-*.d.ts`, `options-*.d.ts`):
- The transport is marked **experimental**. It was added in agents 0.24.0.
- The Durable Object stays in memory, rather than hibernating, while a capnweb connection is open.
- A plain `Agent` answers its own decorated `@callable` methods over the JSON wire and doesn't set `callables`. You only get the native Cap'n Web method behaviour when the host supplies a `callables` `RpcTarget`.

In the `agents` package from 0.23.0 onward, use `this.dynamicAgents.get()` instead of `subAgent()`. The related helpers `hasSubAgent()`, `listSubAgents()`, `abortSubAgent()` and `deleteSubAgent()` are deprecated too. They all still work by calling `this.dynamicAgents` for you, and they don't raise errors or warnings, so old code keeps running and you can migrate when it suits you.

```tsx
const chat = useAgentChat({ agent, throttle: false });
```

Since `agents` 0.22.0, `useAgentChat` batches streaming updates and re-renders every 50 ms by default, so you won't see each token as it arrives. This project has `agents` 0.27.0 installed, so that default applies here. With `throttle: false` the UI renders every chunk as it comes in. You can also pass a number to set a different batching interval in milliseconds, for example `throttle: 16`.

In the installed version (agents 0.27.0), `Agent` extends Cloudflare's `DurableObject<Env>` directly. I confirmed this in the package's type declarations (`node_modules/agents/dist/agent-routing-Bhdbvf7s.d.ts:4521`). Before 0.22.0, `Agent` extended `Server` from `partyserver`, which in turn extended `DurableObject`. That PartyServer runtime is now bundled inside the package under `agents/lifecycle`, so `Agent` is still a Durable Object but no longer sits on top of a `partyserver` class.

In the installed agents 0.27.0, `agents/schedules` has one runtime export: the `Scheduler` class. It's a reusable lifecycle capability for persistent callbacks that fire after a delay, at a set date, on a cron schedule or on an interval. The rest of its exports are TypeScript types: `Schedule`, `ScheduleCriteria`, `ScheduleOptions`, `SchedulerCallbacks`, `SchedulerEventType`, `SchedulerHandlers`, `SchedulerOptions` and `SchedulerPayload` (from `node_modules/agents/dist/schedules/index.d.ts`).

A separate subpath, `agents/schedules/parser`, exports `ParsedSchedule`, `getSchedulePrompt` and `scheduleSchema`.

Yes. In the installed `agents` 0.27.0, a scheduled callback is called as `handler(payload, schedule)`. The first argument is the payload you passed to `this.schedule(when, "callbackName", payload)`. The second is the `Schedule` object for the run, which carries fields like `id` and `callback` plus the timing. You can see the call at `node_modules/agents/dist/scheduler-DZ3xQfeK.js:229`. Schedules routed from a sub-agent go through `_executeRouted` (line 417), which also builds a `Schedule` object before calling the handler.

In the installed `agents` 0.27.0, you don't pass storage to `MCPClientManager`. It extends `LifecycleCapability`, and its constructor only takes `(name, version, options?)`, where `options` holds just `env` and `createAuthProvider`. When the Durable Object lifecycle installs it (for example as `agent.mcp`), it gets the host Durable Object's `DurableObjectStorage` through `this.lifecycle.storage` (`LifecycleServices.storage`).

It uses that storage for three things:
- **Server list:** it keeps the `cf_agents_mcp_servers` table through `storage.sql.exec`, plus a schema-version key.
- **OAuth:** it builds its `DurableObjectOAuthClientProvider` on the same storage.
- **Renames:** it moves OAuth keys when a server id changes.

This is from the installed package's type definitions and compiled code (`node_modules/agents/dist/client-1tEQ1Oqz.js:1304-1353`). Older examples that pass storage into the constructor don't match this version.

The function is `wrapAISDK`, imported from `agents/observability/ai`. You pass it the AI SDK namespace and it returns the same namespace with tracing added (for example, `const ai = wrapAISDK(await import("ai"))`). It works with AI SDK v6 and v7. Its optional second argument, `AISDKInstrumentationOptions`, has three settings: `storeMessages` and `storeTools`, which both default to `false`, and `includeRuntimeContext`, which picks the context keys to record as `cloudflare.agents.runtime_context.*` attributes. The declaration is in `node_modules/agents/dist/observability/ai/index.d.ts:24` in the installed agents 0.27.0.

Yes, that's expected in vitest 5. This project has vitest 5.0.3 installed. According to the project's Ludion lessons file (`.ludion/lessons.md`), vitest 5.0.0 stopped picking up a config file from a parent directory when you run it from a subdirectory. Earlier versions did, so setups that relied on that now lose the root config without any error or warning.

To fix it, pass the config explicitly, for example `npx vitest --config ../../vitest.config.ts` from `packages/foo`. Yes, partly. I checked the Vitest 5.0.3 installed in this project (`node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/index.C4tKZ0yW.js:1906`). If you forget to `await` an `expect(...).resolves` or `expect(...).rejects` assertion, the test fails with an error: "Promise returned by `expect(...).resolves...` was not awaited". Forgetting to `await` `expect.poll(...)` or `expect.element(...)` fails the same way (line 7636).

Vitest only catches those built-in async matchers, though. If your assertion sits inside your own async function, a `.then()` callback or a `setTimeout` that you never awaited, Vitest has no idea it's pending. The test finishes before the assertion runs, so it passes. That's probably what happened to you.

Two things help:
- **`expect.assertions(n)` or `expect.hasAssertions()`** at the top of the test fails it if the expected assertions never ran.
- **The `vitest/valid-expect` rule from `eslint-plugin-vitest`** flags a missing `await` before you even run the tests.

Vitest browser mode supports three providers:

- **Playwright** (`@vitest/browser-playwright`): runs Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. It's the recommended choice for CI and parallel runs.
- **WebdriverIO** (`@vitest/browser-webdriverio`): runs Chrome, Firefox, Edge and Safari through WebDriver.
- **Preview** (`@vitest/browser-preview`): opens the tests in your real local browser. It's only meant for local development and doesn't support headless mode or CI.

Since Vitest 4, you choose one by importing its factory function and passing it to `test.browser.provider`, for example `provider: playwright()`. Before that, you passed a string such as `'playwright'`.

This answer is from my own knowledge of Vitest 4. I didn't check it against the vitest 5.0.3 installed here, and the project's notes on 5.x changes don't mention providers.

The runner code now appears to be bundled into `vitest` itself; `vitest/dist` has `runtime.js` and `task-utils.js` entry points. I'm inferring that from the package contents, not from a changelog. Use `toMatchTextContent`: `await expect.element(el).toMatchTextContent('phrase')`. It also accepts a RegExp, such as `/phrase/i` for a case-insensitive match.

Don't use `toHaveTextContent` for this. In the installed vitest 5.x it only passes when the text matches exactly, so a partial phrase fails. Older code written for the earlier partial-match behaviour won't throw an error; those assertions will just start failing. The installed types say the same thing (`node_modules/@vitest/browser/jest-dom.d.ts:408`).

I can't confirm that Vitest 5 changed how `getByText` matches. The project's Ludion lessons for vitest 5.0.3 mention a nearby change: the browser-mode matcher `toHaveTextContent` now requires an exact match, and `toMatchTextContent` does a partial match. If your check is really `expect(el).toHaveTextContent('Save')` against "Save changes", that change explains the failure. Switch to `toMatchTextContent('Save')` to keep the partial match.

If the locator itself is what fails, check which `getByText` you're calling. Vitest's browser `page.getByText` (Playwright-style) does a case-insensitive substring match unless you pass `{ exact: true }`. `@testing-library`'s `getByText` matches the full string by default, so it needs `/Save/` or `{ exact: false }` to match "Save changes". I haven't looked at your test code, so I don't know which case you're in.

In the vitest version installed here (5.0.3), `vitest --merge-reports` reads from `.vitest/blob/` by default. The blob reporter writes there by default too. I checked this in the installed package: `node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/cac.DfDGTQ9W.js` falls back to `".vitest/blob"` when you don't give a path, and the type definitions list `.vitest/blob` as the default. Config written for those versions still works on 5.x, and the flag is now just redundant. If you want a project to *not* inherit root settings, you'd now opt out explicitly, presumably with `extends: false`.

For the vitest 5.0.3 this project uses, `testNamePattern` (`-t`) is matched against the full test name. That name is the enclosing suite names plus the test name, joined with `" > "` (space, greater-than, space), which is the same string the reporter prints, e.g. `math > add > handles negatives`. Older Vitest versions joined the names with a single space (`math add handles negatives`), so patterns written for that format may silently stop matching after an upgrade.

I didn't check this myself: the `" > "` behaviour comes from the project's `.ludion/lessons.md` notes, and Vitest isn't in `node_modules` here, so I couldn't confirm it against the installed source. If it matters, run `vitest -t "suite > test"` once to see that it matches.

**Not forever, as long as you keep a test timeout.** The test will still fail, but `expect.poll`'s own `timeout` probably isn't what stops it.

- **Why the poll timeout may not fire:** I'm going from my memory of Vitest's source and didn't check it against 5.0.3. As I recall, `expect.poll` awaits your callback on every attempt. When its `timeout` (default 1000 ms) runs out, it makes one last attempt and awaits that too. If your callback returns a promise that never settles, the poll may never resolve or reject.
- **What actually stops it:** the test-level timeout (`testTimeout`, default 5000 ms) still applies and fails the test with a timeout error. It only really hangs forever if you set `testTimeout: 0` or pass a timeout of 0 to that test.
- **How to protect yourself:** make the callback itself time-bounded, for example by wrapping the inner call in `Promise.race` with a short timeout or using an `AbortSignal`. Also always `await expect.poll(...)`. An un-awaited poll can let the test finish early or surface failures in the wrong place.

Yes. Vitest 5.0 added `vi.when`, and this project has vitest 5.0.3 installed, so you can use it. I confirmed it in the installed type definitions (`node_modules/vitest/dist/index.d.ts`). It takes a spy and lets you set results per argument, much like jest-when:

```ts
const spy = vi.fn()
vi.when(spy).calledWith(1).thenReturn(0)
vi.when(spy).calledWith('user').thenResolve({ id: 1 })
```

You can also pass `{ onUnmatched: 'throw' }` so a call with arguments you didn't set up throws an error. On Vitest versions before 5, use `mockImplementation` and branch on the arguments yourself.

`vi.mock` isn't a normal runtime call. Vitest moves it to the top of the test file at compile time, before any `import` runs, so the module is already swapped out when your code imports it. That only works when `vi.mock` is written at the top level of the file. Inside `beforeEach`, the mock would only register after the module had been imported, so it couldn't affect it. Recent Vitest versions warn about `vi.mock` calls that aren't at the top level, and a stricter version turns that into an error, which is probably what you're seeing. I haven't checked the exact behaviour in your installed vitest 5.0.3, and the project's lessons file doesn't mention it.

To fix it, use one of these:
- **Mock once, reset per test:** put `vi.mock('./mod')` at the top level. Then in `beforeEach`, set up what each test needs with `vi.mocked(fn).mockReturnValue(...)` and clear it with `vi.resetAllMocks()`.
- **Mock at runtime:** use `vi.doMock('./mod', factory)`, which isn't moved to the top. Then load the module with `await import('./mod')` after that call, and call `vi.resetModules()` between tests.

`vitest --repeats <n>` runs every test n extra times, and it does this whether the test passes or fails. That makes it useful for finding flaky tests, which only fail some of the time. It works differently from `--retry`. `--retry` only re-runs a test after it fails, so one passing run is enough to count it as a pass. With `--repeats`, every run has to succeed.

In vitest 5.x, `-p` is short for `--project`. It limits the run to the named project(s) in a multi-project (workspace) setup. For example, `vitest -p frontend` is the same as `vitest --project frontend`. The flag was added in vitest 5.0.0, which matches the vitest 5.0.3 this project has installed. Older versions don't have it.

In the vitest version installed here (5.0.3), `vitest list` collects tests by **static parsing**. It reads each test file's source and picks out the `describe`/`test`/`it` calls, without importing or running the file. I confirmed this in your `node_modules`: the CLI defines a `--static-parse` option that defaults to `true` (`cac.DfDGTQ9W.js:1340`). When it's on, `collect()` calls `parseSpecifications(files, …)` instead of running the files (`index.DpLw24bj.js:20943`). You can control how many files are parsed at once with `--static-parse-concurrency`.

Because nothing runs, tests created at runtime (for example, inside loops or with computed names) may be missed or shown differently. Pass `--no-static-parse` to go back to the older behaviour, where the files are actually run to collect the tests.
